units.translation: 115-17a. 〈so that〉 of the Ram: in Colchis, where the ram first brought Phrixus and rested. LmP
8 Φρίξου in K

b. [whom once the son of Aeolus:] Dionysius in his Argonautica (32 fg 2 c J.) says that the Ram was Phrixus' guardian, who first perceived the stepmother's plot and advised him to flee; and when the young man was saved by him, the story spread that Phrixus had been brought safely to Colchis on a ram. 125. rising: ascending. LgP
131-35a. they heard, who also much: he uses hyperbole regarding quantity, if indeed he says that the voice of the dragon is heard by those far from the Colchians, but not by them.

b. far from Titanian Aea: of the Titan river, from which the land is also called Titanis; Eratosthenes mentions it in his Geography (fg III B 76 Berger). The Lycus river, flowing from the Araxes, mingles with the Phasis, and thus losing its own name it flows into the sea. The same thing happens with the Onochonus in Thessaly and the Peneius and the Pamisus; for when they flow together, they are called Peneius. The Araxes is a river of Scythia. Metrodorus in the first book of his On Tigranes (184 fg 1 J.) says that the Thermodon is called Araxes. He says the Caucasian sea is the Caspian because it borders the Caucasus.

b. 〈they whirl:〉 in the rising; and by "another swiftly rises after another" he indicates the continuity of the rising.
c. with whirlings: with the whirlings and twistings of the violent smoke.
d. lifted up: on high. LgP
e. 〈rising up:〉 it is also written "darting." Lm

143-44a. shook countless: many. He has said this hyperbolically, describing the monster of the dragon. "Whirlings" are the coilings of the spiral, the rotations. — And Euripides in Peirithous (fg 593 N.²): "you, the self-born, all [gods] aether with a whirl," that is, in motion, whence also the little wheel moved by sorceresses is called a "rhombus." And in Eupolis (fg 72 Kock I 274): "O rhombus, having whipped me," thus they call circular motions.
